newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich re-election seen as U.S. House vote nears.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich re-election seen as U.S. House vote nears.

text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich seeks re-election by the House on Tuesday to his leadership position under an ethical cloud and facing defections by at least four of his fellow Republicans.
Republican leaders predicted victory for Gingrich in a vote to take place shortly after the new Congress convenes.

But leaders were continuing to try to line up undecided members following a nearly four-hour meeting on Monday night at which Gingrich answered questions from his colleagues about his admitted violation of House ethics rules.
Four Republicans, including Banking Committee Chairman James Leach of Iowa, have said they will not vote for Gingrich and others say they have not made up their minds.

But Ohio Republican Representative John Boehner, chairman of the House Republican Conference, told reporters: "I really do expect tomorrow that there will be no question that Newt Gingrich will be the first Republican speaker re-elected in 68 years."

Republicans, with a 19-vote majority in the House, cannot afford to lose many votes. Democrats will vote for their leader Richard Gephardt. If only 10 Republicans vote for a Republican other than Gingrich, he would not get the overall majority he needs and an additional ballot would be required.

Boehner said Gingrich would win on the first ballot. But he said party leaders would continue to seek out undecided members to try to nail down their votes and that the party would meet again on Tuesday in advance of the election.
In addition to Leach, the publicly announced defectors are Reps. Michael Forbes of New York, Linda Smith of Washington and Tom Campbell of California, all newcomers.
Smith said she might vote for Leach as speaker, and Leach's office said he might vote for another, unnamed, Republican.
"We were told we were not loyal ... and they will keep coming at us until they get the votes," Smith told reporters as she emerged from the meeting.
Representative Ray LaHood, Republican of Illinois, said Republican leaders had discouraged people from voting for others, a point that was "made very strongly" by Republican Whip Tom DeLay."
The session was the first in which Gingrich faced all House Republicans since he acknowledged on December 21 that he had broken House ethics rules.
Many members appeared sombre as they emerged. Gingrich made no statement.

Gingrich has admitted that he brought discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent the use of tax-exempt donations in a partisan political activity -- a college course he taught -- and by misleading ethics committee investigators looking into the matter.

The committee begins work on Wednesday on the punishment phase of the investigation and is widely predicted to recommend that the House vote on a reprimand, the third-severest penalty, later this month.
In a statement issued on Monday, Leach said that any House speaker "must be free of any shadow concerning allegiance to the law or to the truth.
"Accordingly, for the country's sake I have concluded that the most responsible course of action for the speaker is to step down and for the members to choose another leader for the House," he said.
